title: AI Won't Replace Me!
subtitle: Except maybe it will?
body_html:
Dear readers, I've been spending a lot of time thinking about artificial intelligence. I have 2 x 9-year-old twins. What's the future gonna look like for them? This is a meditation on that topic.

Advertising Moment: Inessential Pharmacology

I have a new, PHYSICAL, IN-PRINT book available for purchase. Inessential Pharmacology is available from Amazon (affiliate link), in both hardback and paperback. Kindle ebook version is also available.

Every time I try to use AI chatbots to attempt to get work done, I get disappointed. I know it's supposed to be the future. And I'm trying to get on board with the AI future. But as many of you have probably noticed, once you try to get something complicated done, it just can't.

And the fact that it can't—AI crapped out after a couple of back-and-forths—has to do with something called the content window. The short-term memory of artificial intelligence is limited. The conversation can't go on for that long; it forgets, like a demented adult. You will have a back-and-forth, you'll be working on something, maybe you're me, and you're trying to get it to do an outline of a book. And then it just forgets everything you talked about previously, and craps out something else.

That's probably running out of tokens. Tokens are the unit of computational measure in an AI model, and they turn out to be expensive.

I have a friend who served as a C-level officer for an AI-enough company. In a conversation we had, he mentioned that the capital expenditures associated with building a major AI company are actually pretty similar to those of other capital-intensive businesses, like brick-and-mortar medical clinics, which are the mainstay of medical businesses.

This is very different from prior waves of technology investment. The point of prior venture capital funding into software companies was that they could “endlessly scale.” I'm gonna bring you into the economics of what's happening here, for a second, because it helps us understand the problem with the future of AI everything.

When you're building a company, you're concerned about two crucial numbers.

  1. First is your customer acquisition cost. This is abbreviated CAC.

  2. The second is the customer's long-term value. This is abbreviated LTV.

The number you're trying to optimize is the CAC-to-LTV ratio.

If that ratio is something like 3 to 1, e.g., for every 1 dollar you put into advertising and acquiring a customer, you get 3 dollars of long-term value, and that's a pretty good deal. It makes sense to spend endless money on advertising if the market is large, and for each additional dollar you spend, you get three dollars out.

Businesses like Coca-Cola have really high long-term value to customers, in part because the profit margins on their core product, sugar syrup, are really high. If your profit margins are really thin, let's say you only make 10% profit on whatever you're selling, then you can afford to spend less on customer acquisition.

If you sell high-ticket items with very high margins, you can afford to spend a lot on customer acquisition. Let's take a look at some examples: Facebook sells your time and attention to its advertisers. You, clicking on an ad on Instagram, are the product.

It turns out your time is pretty cheap on Facebook, and we spend a lot of our lives wasting our &%^*& time on their products. (I am not going to bother with the fact that I read a post, because I don't care. It's going to make the point for me, directionally.

Facebook currently has 2.11 billion daily active users (DAUs) on average. The average American user spends approximately 30.9 minutes per day on Facebook, we can assume it’s about 30 minutes per day for the rest of the world as well.

Instagram has 2 billion monthly active users (MAUs). Although recent data on daily active users is not provided, we can use historical information to make an educated estimate. In 2017, when Instagram had 800 million MAUs, it reported 500 million DAUs. Assuming a similar ratio, we can estimate that the current number of daily active users is around 1.25 billion. Users spend an average of 33.9 minutes per day on Instagram.

This translates into a lot of revenue for Meta, which increases on a yearly basis:

Wow, what a great business. But now I'm gonna do some math that's gonna make you sad. 42.375 billion minutes a year on Instagram plus 65.119 billion minutes per year on Facebook. This means something like 107.5 billion minutes of our lives worldwide are spent on meta products in 2025.

What luck, I happen to have a screenshot of their 2025 consolidated financials!

That means Meta makes about $0.2 in profit per minute of our lives they utilize, all told. It's a profitable business.

However, it could be way more profitable if they didn't spend all that money on the metaverse. Also, a few of us would work for the $12/hr we make at Meta. Meta is a software and, fundamentally, an advertising business with strong profit margins. But AI does not have great profit margins, at least not yet.

Those data centers are expensive. They require a ton of expenditures, and they're beholden to purchasing chips from Nvidia, which are also expensive. They require water for cooling. They need electricity on a larger scale than current power plants can provide.

All of those resources mean that the capital expenditures of using an AI model may not be immediately visible to the user, but at least right now, all of us using AI to try to get our work done are being subsidized, massively, by the companies building those tools for us, and selling them at a fraction of the cost.

And that isn’t worth it…unless AI enthusiasts are correct. This was all an open question for me. Then I downloaded Claude Code.

That book I mentioned at the top? It took over a year to get to you, dear readers. Why did it take so long? Cause I needed to reformat a bunch of pictures that got to the ebook version just fine. I couldn’t figure it out. I was unable to figure it out on my own. Claude Code walked me through how to do it, and now it exists in the real world. To be clear, AI didn’t write the book—it just fixed the image files.

Agentic AI is here, it’s real, and it super-powers individuals; it’s not obvious to me. It’s like a giant instruction manual that can also carry them out. It is now pretty clear to me that AI is going to be a huge technology. Chatbots are good, but agents? Holy cow.

AI will absolutely replace a lot of things I do every day, but I would rather not be doing. It is already doing so. That will, predictably, change me.

And it will change you, and it will change our kids. It will replace us with our future selves, who will have to think hard to imagine how it used to be. Savor this moment, the end of an era—it will never be so hard to do boring things ever again.

My kids will, I hope, one day read the things I’ve read instead of having them turned into personal YouTube videos. I also realize I don’t get to say what happens in the future. We get to make choices today—and if we are lucky, tomorrow. My twins will make their own decisions.
